nodes.label: Client application
nodes.summary: Uses a REST API: PUT/GET/DELETE on bucket + key, LIST by prefix, multipart upload.
nodes.details: Objects are addressed by bucket + key (+ version). Updates to one key are atomic. There are no atomic multi-key updates.

nodes.label: Front-end fleet
nodes.summary: Stateless API tier: authenticates, routes to metadata and storage.
nodes.details: AWS says S3 is made of hundreds of microservices. The exact front-end layout is not public, so this box is a generic stand-in.

nodes.label: Metadata / index
nodes.summary: Maps bucket + key + version to the object's shard locations. Cached for availability. Object becomes visible only when its metadata exists.
nodes.details: Vogels describes a metadata cache and a persistence tier. 'Commit metadata last' is the standard design, not a published S3 detail.

nodes.label: Cache coherence witness
nodes.summary: Notified on every object change. Acts as a read barrier so a cache can tell whether its copy is stale. This gave strong read-after-write consistency without lowering availability.
nodes.details: Dec 2020: strong read-after-write consistency for all requests, at no extra charge and with no performance impact (AWS announcement).

nodes.label: Storage nodes (ShardStore)
nodes.summary: HDD nodes running ShardStore, written in Rust (>40,000 lines). Per-node LSM tree maps shard IDs to chunks held in extents, with shard data stored outside the tree.
nodes.details: Writes within an extent are sequential. Validated with executable reference models (about 1% of the code) and property-based tests.

nodes.label: Erasure coding
nodes.summary: Splits an object into k data shards plus m parity shards. Any k of the k+m shards reconstruct it. Exact k and m for S3 are not public.
nodes.details: Warfield names Reed-Solomon as an example and gives no k or m values. Any numbers in this atlas's examples are illustrative.

nodes.label: Spread across ≥3 AZs
nodes.summary: Standard classes store across at least three AZs and are designed to survive the loss of one. One Zone-IA uses a single AZ.

nodes.label: Scrubber / repair
nodes.summary: Background processes verify checksums and quickly repair lost redundancy. Durability depends on repair speed versus drive failure rate.
nodes.details: AWS: designed to handle concurrent device failures by quickly detecting and repairing any lost redundancy, and regularly verifying integrity with checksums. The exact scrubber implementation is not described.

steps.caption: The client sends the object with PUT. Large objects use multipart upload (parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB).
The data is erasure coded into k data shards plus m parity shards (Reed-Solomon is the named example).
Shards are written in parallel to different drives on ShardStore nodes.
Placement spreads them across failure domains, at least three AZs for standard classes.
Only after the data is durable is the metadata committed. The object becomes visible when its metadata exists. This ordering is the standard design, not a published S3 detail.
The witness acts as a read barrier so the metadata cache can tell whether its copy is fresh.
A fresh cached entry is used. A stale one is invalidated and read from the persistence tier.
Any k of the k+m shards are enough to reconstruct the object, so slow or failed drives can be skipped.
Background verification finds shards that are lost or fail their checksum.
Lost shards are rebuilt from the surviving ones and written to healthy drives, restoring full redundancy. Durability rests on repairing faster than drives fail.
